title: Leaders Who Yell and Ridicule on Purpose
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Using Steve Jobs' notorious tirades at Apple as its opening case, this Admired Leadership piece asks whether raising your voice is ever an effective leadership tactic. Its answer turns on the perceived intentions behind the yelling: mean-spirited anger and humiliation versus passionate caring about an issue. The author concedes that some great leaders yelled and that some arenas, such as athletics and the military, expect it, while insisting that no one ever forgets being screamed at. When intentions are read unfavorably, yelling keeps people on edge and demotivates them; when read as passion, it can add energy and emphasis. The decisive variable, the piece argues, is frequency, since habitual yelling becomes an insult even from leaders known to care.
points: Whether yelling works depends on how its intentions are perceived: disrespect and humiliation versus passion for an important issue.
Yelling perceived as mean-spirited keeps people on edge waiting for the next tirade and demotivates their best work.
Frequency is the key concern: used too often, a raised voice is read as an insult even from leaders known to care.
The Jobs example is treated ironically; habitual screamers are eventually ignored unless, the piece quips, they invent the iPhone.
quotes: In fact, Jobs so frequently lambasted and yelled at colleagues, those on the receiving end would often say they had been “Steved.” When asked about this, Jobs believed his tirades contributed to Apple’s tremendous success. In other words, he did it on purpose.

It depends on the perceived intentions of the screamer. Is the leader yelling to express their anger or disappointment in a mean-spirited and disrespectful way? Or are they yelling because of their passion and caring about the issue at hand?

Some of the best leaders in history were known to yell now and again. In some workplaces, such as athletic and military arenas, it is even expected. That said, one thing is for certain: No one ever forgets getting screamed at.

When a leader’s high-decibel intentions are viewed as unfavorable, yelling keeps everyone on edge, waiting for the next tirade. It alarms people and demotivates them from doing their best work. It feels disrespectful because it is.
The key concern is how frequently a leader raises their voice. Used too often, yelling will almost always be seen as an insult and highly ill-mannered, even when leaders are known to care.
Constantly yelling and carrying on doesn’t make anyone a better leader. What it does make is someone who becomes known as a screamer. And screamers are eventually ignored or marched to the nut house.
